faq.q: Why is CK the first test?

faq.a: Yes, many traditional remedies contain cyanogenic glycosides or heavy metals that damage muscle.
When inflammatory myopathy is likely (proximal weakness, high CK, EMG changes) and infection has been ruled out.

exam: A 35‑year‑old HIV‑positive man on protease inhibitors presents with proximal weakness – what is your next step? — Review medication list, stop the protease inhibitor if possible, check CK and consider steroids if inflammatory pattern.

A patient with severe malaria treated with quinine develops dark urine – how do you differentiate rhabdomyolysis from hematuria? — Perform urine dipstick for blood and myoglobin, check CK; myoglobinuria gives positive dipstick without RBCs on microscopy.

How would you manage a child with suspected congenital muscular dystrophy in a setting without genetic testing? — Focus on supportive physiotherapy, monitor for respiratory complications, and educate family; avoid unnecessary investigations.
What clinical feature helps you separate myopathy from peripheral neuropathy? — Presence of sensory loss points to neuropathy; pure motor weakness with normal sensation suggests myopathy.
Why might CK be normal in early polymyositis and how would you still diagnose it? — Early disease may not cause massive necrosis; rely on EMG, MRI, and clinical pattern.
A patient on high‑dose steroids develops new weakness – what should you consider? — Steroid‑induced myopathy; check CK (usually normal) and taper steroids if possible.
What are the red‑flag signs of life‑threatening myopathy? — Rapid CK rise >10,000, oliguria, hyperkalemia, respiratory muscle weakness.
How does hypothyroidism cause myopathy and what test confirms it? — Thyroid hormone deficiency leads to muscle fiber atrophy; confirm with elevated TSH and low free T4.
ai.title: Myopathy
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Myopathy refers to diseases of skeletal muscle causing weakness, pain or wasting. In low‑resource settings, common causes include infections, toxins, and metabolic disorders. Diagnosis relies on clinical clues and targeted investigations.

b: Acute: often infectious or drug‑induced
Chronic: inflammatory (e.g., polymyositis) or metabolic (e.g., hypothyroidism)
Hereditary: muscular dystrophies, congenital myopathies
sections.p: Myopathy is any primary disorder of muscle fibers leading to reduced strength or endurance. It can be acute or chronic, inflammatory, metabolic, toxic, or hereditary.

b: Symmetric proximal weakness → inflammatory or endocrine
Distal or foot‑drop pattern → peripheral neuropathy or hereditary
Rapid onset with fever → infection or drug toxicity
sections.p: Think of myopathy as a problem of the muscle cell itself, not the nerves. Identify pattern of weakness, associated systemic features, and exposure history.

b: HIV protease inhibitors → mitochondrial toxicity
Malaria treatment (quinine) → rhabdomyolysis
Traditional herbal remedies (e.g., cassava) → cyanide‑related myopathy
sections.p: In East African hospitals, the most frequent myopathies are HIV‑related, antiretroviral toxicity, malaria‑associated rhabdomyolysis, and herbal toxin exposure.
When a test is unavailable, rely on bedside clues (e.g., urine dipstick for myoglobin) and treat presumptively.

t.b: Is there muscle cell injury? – Markedly raised (>5× upper limit) supports myopathy; normal does not exclude mild disease
Is rhabdomyolysis causing AKI? – Elevated potassium, creatinine, low calcium suggest complications
Is the problem myopathic or neurogenic? – Myopathic pattern shows short, low‑amplitude motor units
What is the histologic type? – Inflammatory infiltrates → polymyositis; vacuoles → metabolic
Is HIV‑related myopathy likely? – Positive test with high viral load supports diagnosis
Is hypothyroidism causing myopathy? – Elevated TSH with low free T4 confirms

b: Stop offending drug or toxin immediately
Treat infections (e.g., antimalarials, antibiotics for bacterial myositis)
Start steroids for confirmed inflammatory myopathy unless contraindicated
Hydration and alkalinisation of urine to prevent myoglobin nephropathy
Physiotherapy to maintain muscle strength
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then provide supportive care to prevent complications such as rhabdomyolysis‑induced renal failure.

b: Neuropathy: sensory loss and distal weakness predominate
Myasthenia gravis: fluctuating weakness, ocular involvement, normal CK
Hypokalemia: weakness improves with potassium replacement
sections.p: Distinguish myopathy from neuropathy, myasthenia gravis, and electrolyte‑induced weakness.

b: CK can be falsely low after prolonged immobilisation
Urine dipstick positive for blood may reflect myoglobin, not hematuria
sections.p: CK may be modestly raised in chronic myopathy; normal CK does not rule out early disease. EMG can be normal early on.

b: Ask about recent infections, drug changes, and traditional medicines
Check for calf tenderness, swelling, and dark urine
Perform a quick gait test: difficulty rising from chair suggests proximal weakness
sections.p: Focus on pattern of weakness, systemic clues, and simple bedside tests.

b: Assuming normal CK excludes myopathy
Delaying steroids in inflammatory myopathy due to fear of infection
Neglecting renal protection in rhabdomyolysis
sections.p: Avoid over‑reliance on a single test and missing treatable causes.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe hyperkalemia (>6.0 mmol/L) or cardiac arrhythmia
Progressive weakness leading to respiratory failure
